The galvanometer and the shunt are in **parallel**, so they carry the same voltage and
the currents divide in inverse proportion to the resistances.
**Step 1 — split the main current.** If 10% goes through the galvanometer,
I_g = **0·1 I** and I_s = **0·9 I** ✓
**Step 2 — equate the voltages across the parallel pair.**
I_g G = I_s S
(0·1 I)G = (0·9 I)S
**Step 3 — solve for S.**
S = 0·1G/0·9
= **G/9** ✓
**Why the shunt must be much smaller than G.** It has to carry **nine times** as much
current at the same voltage, so its resistance must be a ninth of the galvanometer's ✓
A shunt is always a thick, low-resistance strip for exactly this reason.
**The general formula.** To pass a fraction 1/n of the main current through the
galvanometer,
**S = G/(n − 1)** ✓
Here n = 10, giving G/9 ✓ and for 1% it would be G/99.
**Why an ammeter needs a shunt at all.** A bare galvanometer is a delicate instrument
that full-scales at a few milliamps ✓ The shunt diverts most of the current around it,
so the combination can measure amperes while the coil still sees only a safe trickle.
**The resistance of the finished ammeter.**
R_A = GS/(G + S) = G(G/9)/(10G/9) = **G/10** ✓
lower than the galvanometer alone, which is exactly what an ammeter needs - it must
disturb the circuit it is inserted into as little as possible.
**The contrast with a voltmeter.** A voltmeter is a galvanometer with a **large**
resistance in **series**, so that it draws almost no current ✓ Shunt for an ammeter,
multiplier for a voltmeter - the two are mirror images.
**Reading the distractors.** **9G** ✗ and **90G** ✗ are larger than G, which would send
**less** current through the shunt than through the galvanometer - the opposite of what
is wanted. **G** ✗ would split the current equally, giving 50%, not 10% ✓
∴ G/9.

Adding identical cells in series raises the emf and the internal resistance **in the same
proportion**, so the short-circuit current does not change.
**Step 1 — write the emf of n cells in series.**
E_total = **nE** ✓
**Step 2 — write their total internal resistance.**
r_total = **nr** ✓
**Step 3 — find the short-circuit current.** With the terminals joined by a wire of
negligible resistance, the only resistance in the circuit is the cells' own:
I = E_total/r_total
= nE/(nr)
= **E/r** ✓
**Step 4 — read off the graph.** The n cancels completely, so I is **independent of n** ✓
The graph is a **horizontal straight line** - the third option.
**Why the cancellation happens.** Each extra cell contributes an emf E that pushes the
current **up**, and an internal resistance r that holds it **down**, and for a short
circuit the two effects are exactly equal ✓ Nothing is gained by adding cells.
**What would change the answer.** If an **external** resistance R were present,
I = nE/(R + nr) ✓
which **rises** with n and saturates at E/r - that is the second graph, and the
distractor it provides. The phrase "terminals are short-circuited" sets R = 0 and is the
key to the question.
**A worked instance.** With E = 1·5 V and r = 0·5 Ω:
one cell: I = 1·5/0·5 = **3 A**
five cells: I = 7·5/2·5 = **3 A** ✓
twenty cells: I = 30/10 = **3 A** ✓ unchanged throughout.
**Why cells are put in series at all.** To raise the voltage available to an **external**
load ✓ With R ≫ nr the current is approximately nE/R, growing nearly in proportion to n -
which is the whole point of a battery of cells.
**Reading the distractors.** The **rising** curves ✗ describe the case with an external
resistance, and the **falling** line ✗ would need the internal resistance to grow faster
than the emf, which identical cells cannot do ✓
∴ the horizontal line - the current is independent of n.

The force on a current-carrying wire is **F = BIl sin θ**, so a segment **parallel** to B
feels nothing.
**Step 1 — read the geometry.** The field B points **horizontally to the right**. The
wire runs from P horizontally to Q, then turns and runs vertically up to R, with
PQ = QR = l ✓
**Step 2 — find the force on PQ.** This segment lies **along** the field, so the angle
between the current and B is **zero**:
F_PQ = BIl sin 0°
= **0** ✓
**Step 3 — find the force on QR.** This segment is **perpendicular** to the field:
F_QR = BIl sin 90°
= **BIl** ✓
**Step 4 — give the pair in the order asked.** The force on PQ and on QR is
**0, BIl** ✓
**Why a parallel wire feels no force.** The magnetic force is F̄ = I l̄ x B̄, a cross
product, which vanishes when the two vectors are **parallel** ✓ Physically, the moving
charges in PQ travel along the field lines, and a charge moving along B experiences no
magnetic force at all.
**The direction of the force on QR.** By F̄ = I l̄ x B̄ with the current upward and B to
the right, the force is directed **into the page** ✓ perpendicular to both.
**A useful shortcut for bent wires.** The total force on any wire between two points
depends only on the **straight line joining them**:
F = BI L_effective ✓
Here the straight line from P to R has length l√2, but its component perpendicular to B
is just l - giving a total force BIl, consistent with the segment-by-segment result.
**Reading the distractors.** **BIl, 0** ✗ has the two segments swapped - it would be
right if B were vertical. **2BIl, 0** ✗ doubles a force that is zero to begin with.
**0, 0** ✗ would need the field parallel to both segments, which is impossible for two
perpendicular wires ✓
∴ 0, BIl.

A choke limits current **without dissipating energy**, which a resistor cannot do.
**Step 1 — see how each limits the current.**
a **resistor** limits it by opposing the flow and turning the lost energy into **heat**
a **choke** - a coil of large inductance - limits it by its **reactance** X_L = ωL ✓
**Step 2 — compare the power each consumes.** The average power in an a.c. circuit is
P = V_rms I_rms cos φ
For a resistor, φ = 0 and cos φ = **1**, so it consumes power continuously
For an ideal choke, φ = **90°** and cos φ = **0**, so it consumes **no average power at
all** ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** The choke is preferred because there is **no wastage of power** ✓
**Where the energy goes instead.** During one quarter-cycle the choke stores energy in
its **magnetic field**, ½LI², and during the next it returns that energy to the source ✓
Averaged over a cycle the net transfer is zero - energy is borrowed and repaid, never
consumed.
**A worked comparison.** To limit a 230 V supply to 2 A:
a **resistor** of 115 Ω dissipates 2²(115) = **460 W** as heat
a **choke** of the same reactance dissipates, ideally, **0 W** ✓
The saving is the whole of the 460 W, which is why fluorescent lamps have used chokes
for a century.
**Why a choke works only on a.c.** Its reactance is ωL, which is **zero** for direct
current ✓ On d.c. a choke is just a coil of wire with a little resistance, and limits
nothing.
**The practical caveat.** A real choke has some winding resistance and some iron loss,
so cos φ is small but not zero ✓ It still wastes far less than an equivalent resistor.
**Reading the distractors.** **Cheap** ✗ - a choke with an iron core costs **more** than
a resistor. **Compact** ✗ - it is usually **bulkier**. **Absorbs heat** ✗ - the point is
that it does not **produce** heat ✓
∴ there is no wastage of power.

The current entering at P has two routes to R, and it divides in **inverse** proportion
to their resistances.
**Step 1 — identify the two paths from P to R.**
direct, along PR: one side of the triangle, **2 Ω**
round the other way, P → Q → R: two sides, **2 + 2 = 4 Ω** ✓
These two paths are in **parallel** between P and R.
**Step 2 — divide the current in inverse proportion.** The 6 A splits so that the
**easier** path takes the larger share:
through the 2 Ω path: 6 x 4/(2 + 4) = 6 x (2/3) = **4 A**
through the 4 Ω path: 6 x 2/(2 + 4) = 6 x (1/3) = **2 A** ✓
**Step 3 — assign them to the figure.** I₁ is the current round the long way through Q,
and I₂ the direct current to R, so
**I₁ = 2 A, I₂ = 4 A** ✓
**Step 4 — check.** 2 + 4 = **6 A** ✓ all the current entering at P leaves at R, as it
must.
**The current-divider rule.** For two parallel branches,
I₁ = I x R₂/(R₁ + R₂) ✓
The branch's **own** resistance appears in the **denominator** only - the numerator
carries the **other** branch's resistance. Getting that the wrong way round is the
commonest error, and it turns 2 A into 4 A.
**A check by voltages.** The potential difference between P and R must be the same by
either route:
direct: 4 A x 2 Ω = **8 V**
long way: 2 A x 4 Ω = **8 V** ✓ equal, as Kirchhoff's loop rule requires.
**The equivalent resistance between P and R.**
R_PR = (2 x 4)/(2 + 4) = **4/3 Ω** ✓
and a check: 6 A x 4/3 Ω = **8 V** ✓ the same potential difference.
**Why symmetry alone does not settle it.** The triangle is symmetric in its
**resistances**, but the current enters and leaves at two particular corners, which
breaks the symmetry ✓ Q carries only the 2 A that goes the long way.
**Reading the distractors.** **4 A, 2 A** ✗ swaps the two - it assigns the larger current
to the longer path. **1 A, 2 A** ✗ and **2 A, 3 A** ✗ do not even sum to 6 A ✓
∴ 2 A, 4 A.

First test whether the bridge is **balanced**; then the galvanometer branch can be
ignored and the two arms treated as a simple parallel pair.
**Step 1 — test for balance.**
P/Q = 10/20 = **0·5**
R/S = 15/30 = **0·5** ✓
The ratios are equal, so the bridge is **balanced**: the two midpoints are at the same
potential and **no current flows through the galvanometer** ✓
**Step 2 — remove the galvanometer.** With no current in it, the branch may be deleted
without changing anything else ✓ The network becomes two series arms in parallel across
the battery.
**Step 3 — find each arm.** As the figure is drawn, P and R lie in one arm and Q and S
in the other:
arm 1: P + R = 10 + 15 = **25 Ω**
arm 2: Q + S = 20 + 30 = **50 Ω**
**Step 4 — combine them in parallel.**
R_eq = (25 x 50)/(25 + 50)
= 1250/75
= **16·67 Ω**
**Step 5 — find the current from the battery.**
I = E/R_eq
= 6/16·67
= **0·36 A** ✓
**How the current splits between the arms.**
through the 25 Ω arm: 6/25 = **0·24 A**
through the 50 Ω arm: 6/50 = **0·12 A**
total: **0·36 A** ✓ consistent.
**Why balance makes the problem easy.** An unbalanced bridge needs Kirchhoff's laws and
three simultaneous equations ✓ A balanced one collapses to series and parallel
combinations, because the galvanometer branch carries nothing and can be cut out - or
equally, short-circuited, with the same result.
**Why the galvanometer's resistance never appears.** No current passes through it, so
whatever its resistance, it drops no voltage and affects nothing ✓ That independence is
precisely what makes the Wheatstone bridge such an accurate instrument.
**Reading the distractors.** **0 A** ✗ confuses the **galvanometer** current, which is
indeed zero, with the **battery** current, which is not. **0·72 A** ✗ is twice the
answer and **0·18 A** ✗ half ✓
∴ 0.36 A.

Heating a metal raises its **resistance**, which cuts the current and so the drift
velocity - while the random thermal motion speeds up.
**Step 1 — see what happens to the resistance.** In a metal, lattice ions vibrate more
vigorously as the temperature rises, so electrons collide more often and the **mean free
time τ falls** ✓ Since
ρ = m/(ne²τ)
the resistivity, and hence the resistance, **increases** ✓
**Step 2 — see what happens to the current.** The potential difference is held
**constant**, so by Ohm's law
I = V/R
and with R larger, the current **decreases** ✓
**Step 3 — see what happens to the drift velocity.**
I = neAv_d
so with n, e and A fixed, v_d is proportional to I ✓ The drift velocity therefore
**decreases**.
**Step 4 — see what happens to the thermal velocity.** The random thermal speed of an
electron follows
½mv²_th = (3/2)kT, so **v_th ∝ √T** ✓
Raising the temperature **increases** it.
**Step 5 — conclude.** The drift velocity **decreases** and the thermal velocity
**increases** ✓
**Why the two move in opposite directions.** They are quite different motions ✓
**thermal velocity** is the fast, **random** zig-zag an electron has even with no field -
about **10⁵ m s⁻¹** at room temperature, and set purely by temperature
**drift velocity** is the slow, **directed** crawl superimposed on it by the field -
about **10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹**, and set by the field and the collision time
Heating stirs up the random motion, and that very stirring obstructs the directed one.
**The size of the contrast.** The thermal speed is some **10⁹ times** the drift speed ✓
An electron travels a kilometre of random zig-zag for every millimetre of net progress -
which is why a current appears instantly though the electrons themselves barely move.
**The direct route via τ.** v_d = eEτ/m, and τ falls with temperature, so v_d falls ✓
the same conclusion without mentioning resistance at all.
∴ decreases, thermal velocity of the electron increases.
